hints: Look at the boiling points in the table. Which oxides have very high boiling points near 3000 degrees and which has a very low boiling point of 45 degrees, and what does that tell you about giant vs simple structures?
Recall how bonding changes across Period 3 from left to right, from highly ionic metal oxides to covalent non-metal oxides, and where the changeover occurs.
walkthrough:
Use boiling point as your structure clue**
Think like this: to boil a giant lattice you have to break a huge network of strong bonds, so the boiling point is very high, thousands of degrees. To boil a simple molecular substance you only overcome weak forces between molecules, so the boiling point is low. Here $\text{SO}_3$ boils at only $45^{\circ}\text{C}$, so it must be simple molecular. All the others boil above $1200^{\circ}\text{C}$, so they are all giant.

Track bonding across the period**
Across Period 3 the metal to non-metal character changes. $\text{Na}$, $\text{Mg}$ and $\text{Al}$ are metals forming ionic oxides with $\text{O}^{2-}$, while $\text{Si}$ and $\text{S}$ are non-metals forming covalent oxides. So $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$, $\text{MgO}$, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ are ionic and giant, $\text{SiO}_2$ is covalent and giant, $\text{SO}_3$ is covalent and simple molecular.

Final answer: Bonding: $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ ionic, $\text{MgO}$ ionic, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ ionic, $\text{SiO}_2$ covalent, $\text{SO}_3$ covalent.
Structure: $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ giant, $\text{MgO}$ giant, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ giant, $\text{SiO}_2$ giant / macromolecular, $\text{SO}_3$ simple / molecular.

hints: Recall from part (a) the structure of each oxide: which one is a continuous network and which one exists as separate small molecules?
Identify what must be broken to boil each one: strong covalent bonds throughout the lattice versus weak forces between molecules.
Link strength of attraction to energy needed, and therefore to boiling point.
walkthrough:
Picture what each solid really looks like**
Imagine $\text{SiO}_2$ as an endless 3D scaffolding where every $\text{Si}$ is covalently bonded to four $\text{O}$ atoms and every $\text{O}$ bridges two $\text{Si}$ atoms. There are no separate $\text{SiO}_2$ molecules. Now picture $\text{SO}_3$ as neat little separate $\text{SO}_3$ molecules just sitting next to each other.

Ask what boiling has to break**
To make $\text{SiO}_2$ boil you must snap strong $\text{Si-O}$ covalent bonds throughout that giant network. To make $\text{SO}_3$ boil you do not touch the strong $\text{S-O}$ covalent bonds inside each molecule at all, you only separate one $\text{SO}_3$ molecule from its neighbour by overcoming weak van der Waals forces.

Connect strength to energy and boiling point**
Strong covalent bonds need a huge amount of thermal energy to break, while weak intermolecular forces need very little energy to overcome. That is why $\text{SiO}_2$ boils at $2950^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $\text{SO}_3$ boils at only $45^{\circ}\text{C}$.

Final answer: $\text{SiO}_2$ has a giant covalent network with many strong $\text{Si-O}$ covalent bonds to break.
$\text{SO}_3$ is simple molecular with only weak van der Waals / intermolecular forces between molecules.
Much more energy is required to break the strong covalent bonds in $\text{SiO}_2$ than to overcome the weak intermolecular forces in $\text{SO}_3$, so $\text{SiO}_2$ has a much higher boiling point.

hints: Break the word amphoteric into its meaning: able to behave in two opposite ways toward acids and bases.
Think of a familiar acid reaction of a metal oxide that forms a salt plus water, for example with $\text{HCl}$ or $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$.
Think of the alkali reaction that is special to aluminium, forming the complex ion $[\text{Al}(\text{OH})_4]^-$.
walkthrough:
Pin down the word amphoteric**
Do not overcomplicate it. Amphoteric simply means the oxide can act as a base and as an acid. So it will react with an acid to make a salt, and it will also react with a base or alkali to make a different salt.

Show the basic behaviour with acid**
Acting as a base, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ neutralises acid in the normal oxide plus acid way. For example:
$$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 6\text{HCl} \rightarrow 2\text{AlCl}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Any correct acid equation forming an $\text{Al}^{3+}$ salt plus water is accepted.

Show the acidic behaviour with alkali**
Acting as an acid, it reacts with hot concentrated alkali to give sodium aluminate. For example:
$$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{NaOH} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaAl}(\text{OH})_4$$
The product contains the tetrahydroxoaluminate ion, $[\text{Al}(\text{OH})_4]^-$. Together the two equations prove amphoteric character.

Final answer: Amphoteric means reacts with both acids and bases / alkalis.
With acid, e.g. $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 6\text{HCl} \rightarrow 2\text{AlCl}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$
With alkali, e.g. $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{NaOH} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaAl}(\text{OH})_4$

hints: Recall that $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ is a strongly basic oxide that reacts vigorously and exothermically with water to form a soluble alkali.
walkthrough:
Visualise a basic oxide hitting water**
$\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ reacts as:
$$\text{Na}_2\text{O} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaOH}$$
The solid $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ is used up to make soluble $\text{NaOH}$, so you see the white solid disappear and dissolve. The reaction is strongly exothermic, so the mixture also feels warm or hot.
Final answer: Solid dissolves / disappears (to give colourless solution) OR mixture gets warm / hot.

hints: Count regions of electron density around Se in $\text{SeF}_6$: how many bonding pairs and how many lone pairs are there?
walkthrough:
Apply VSEPR in seconds**
In $\text{SeF}_6$, selenium forms six $\text{Se-F}$ bonds and has no lone pairs left, just like $\text{SF}_6$. Six bonding pairs repel equally to point to the six corners of an octahedron, with $90^{\circ}$ bond angles. So the shape is octahedral.

hints: Write the enthalpy change in terms of bonds: one $\text{Se=O}$ bond is broken and two $\text{Se-O}$ bonds are made, so $\Delta H$ equals energy in for breaking minus energy out for forming.
Substitute $\Delta H = -346 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $E(\text{Se=O}) = 514 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ and solve for $E(\text{Se-O})$, remembering the factor of 2.
walkthrough:
Translate the diagram into bonds**
Look carefully: gaseous $\text{SeO}_2$ has two $\text{Se=O}$ double bonds. In the polymer unit one $\text{Se=O}$ remains and the other $\text{Se=O}$ has been replaced by two $\text{Se-O}$ single bonds. So per mole the net change is: break $1$ mole of $\text{Se=O}$, make $2$ moles of $\text{Se-O}$.

Set up the bond enthalpy equation and solve**
Use $\Delta H$ equals sum of bonds broken minus sum of bonds formed:
$$\Delta H = E(\text{Se=O broken}) - 2E(\text{Se-O formed})$$
$$-346 = 514 - 2E_{\text{Se-O}}$$
Rearrange:
$$2E_{\text{Se-O}} = 514 + 346 = 860$$
$$E_{\text{Se-O}} = 430 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

hints: Recall how the analogous acidic oxide $\text{SO}_2$ reacts with $2\text{NaOH}$ to give sodium sulfite plus water, then replace S by Se.
walkthrough:
Copy the sulfur chemistry across to selenium**
You are told $\text{SeO}_2$ behaves like $\text{SO}_2$. $\text{SO}_2$ is an acidic oxide and with alkali gives a sulfite:
$$\text{SO}_2 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Just swap $\text{S}$ for $\text{Se}$ to get sodium selenite:
$$\text{SeO}_2 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SeO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
The equation is already balanced with $2$ moles of $\text{NaOH}$.
